units: the writer is looking after the dog of a close friend who has gone travelling
the animal whined at night behind the bedroom door
it refused to eat its ration
it damaged the floor with its claws whenever she moved away
the writer first read this behaviour as a reproach
a training specialist explained that the animal was looking for a reassuring fixed point
she was advised to keep walks at regular hours and to place the bed near the entrance
the dog now sleeps against a cloth that holds its owner's scent
text: Your dog has been with me since you set off, and I am writing to you at last as someone who has finally found the way out. For the first few nights he whimpered behind my bedroom door, turned his nose up at his bowl, and raked the floorboards with his claws the moment I stepped away from him. I took all of it as a rebuke for having let you go. A trainer put me right: the animal was hunting for a fixed point, not passing judgement on me. She told me to walk him at the same hours every day, and to shift his bed against the wall by the front door. He settles there now as soon as the light goes, curls against the cloth that still holds your scent, and waits for the latch without a murmur. He eats, he runs, and he sleeps deeply. You will come home to a calm companion, and to a rather proud friend.

units: specialists in animal behaviour refuse to treat the two kinds of group as one
in a group of grass-eaters each beast takes its cue from its nearest neighbours
no member of that group holds an overall view of the manoeuvre
among bees scouts come back and pass on directions through their movements
the colony settles on the site that gathers the most support
the first group exchanges bodily stances and changes of pace
the second group exchanges content comparable to a reasoned proposal
the first reacts almost instantly whereas the second takes several days to decide
text: Should a herd and a swarm be thought of as two settings on the same machine? Specialists in animal behaviour will not have it. Within a herd, each beast takes its cue from the animals immediately beside it, and the shape of the whole comes out of those local corrections; not one of them holds the manoeuvre in mind. A swarm works on quite another principle. Scouts return and pass on directions through the way they move, and the colony settles on whichever site gathers the most support. So what divides the two? What travels between the members. A herd passes on a stance, a quickening pace, a turn of the head. A swarm passes on something closer to a case being argued. And the pace of it? A herd answers within a fraction of a second, while a swarm weighs the matter for days before it lifts off.

units: a stock keeper set out her worries to a veterinary practitioner
she reported that the animals had been eating less grass for a week
she added that the chewing of the cud lasted a shorter time than usual
the practitioner examined the teeth of the animals
he then checked the quality of the water made available
he also judged the fodder too poor in fibre
he recommended keeping the weakened animals apart from the group
he promised to come back and check the state of the herd
text: The stock keeper set out her worries at some length to the vet who had come out to look over her animals. She told him the cattle had been cropping less grass for a week, and that they stopped chewing the cud sooner than they used to. The vet said he would work through three lines of enquiry in turn. He began with the teeth of each animal, since a single broken one is enough to put a beast off chewing. He then drew water from the trough, whose pipe struck him as clogged. Last, he judged the fodder too poor in fibre, and so ill suited to their digestion. Before leaving, he advised her to keep the weaker animals apart from the rest, to write down every refused feed, and to ring the surgery if intake did not pick up. He gave his word that he would come back before long and check on the state of the herd.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the drawing together of humans and wild animals began with a mutual acceptance
meat-eaters came to look for the waste left around the camps
the least wary individuals ended up being fed
hunting bands mixing humans and dog-like animals took shape
grass-eaters were then penned as a living store of food
these beasts were picked over for their steadiness and their fleece
the rise of sown crops created a need for animals able to pull loads
cats were suffered in order to keep gnawing creatures away from the grain stores
text: Domestication began with no decision behind it, only with a mutual putting up with. Meat-eaters prowled at the edge of hunting camps, drawn by the scraps thrown aside; the wariest slipped away, the boldest lingered and ended up being fed. Out of that closeness came the mixed band, human and dog-like animal running down game together. Grass-eaters were penned next, held at first as a larder on the hoof, then picked over for their steadiness and for the thickness of their fleece. Sown fields, once they spread, called for pulling power, and the sturdiest beasts were harnessed to the plough. Later still, cats were suffered in the grain stores, where they held the gnawing creatures away from the harvest. Every stage lengthened the roll of species bound to us, and reshaped their outline as much as their temper.

units: a thin see-through covering left by a reptile is sometimes found on the ground
the outer layer of a snake's skin does not stretch as the animal grows longer
that stiffness forces the reptile to get rid of its old covering
a fresh layer builds up beneath the old one
a fluid seeps in between the two layers and lifts them apart
the eyes of the animal turn cloudy during this phase
the snake hunts little and hides while its sight is poor
it rubs its snout against a stone to start the lifting
text: Have you ever picked up one of those see-through papery things by the side of a path and wondered what creature could have left it there? That is a snake skin, and the whole business comes down to a fault in the design. The outer layer that shields the reptile will not stretch, while the animal underneath keeps getting longer. So, sooner or later, it has to shed. A fresh layer builds up below the old one, then a fluid seeps in between the two and lifts them apart. While that goes on, the eyes cloud over to a milky blue and the poor thing can barely see. It hardly hunts at all, and tucks itself away under a stump. Once the split is complete, it rubs its snout on a rough stone, catches the rim of the old covering, and works its way out of it. What you find lying on the ground is that worn out coat.

units: a mark left in the mud near a pen set off alarm
ewes had been killed during the night
the sheep farmers put the losses down to a wild meat-eater
a naturalist judged the mark too broad for that explanation
cameras triggered by movement were set up
the pictures showed two dogs without an owner at hand
the owners of the dogs were traced and held responsible
an electrified fence and a watch kept at night put an end to the raids
text: The alarm went up over a single print in the mud, a few steps away from a pen where three ewes had been killed during the night. Sheep farmers round the valley pointed straight at a wild meat-eater and asked for leave to shoot it. A naturalist sent out to look refused to sign up to that. The pad mark seemed too broad to her, and the bites fell in the wrong places for a practised hunter. She had cameras set up along the fences, the sort that trip of their own accord when something moves. The pictures, collected the week after, showed two stray dogs with collars round their necks, no owner anywhere near. The men who kept them were traced and held to account for the losses. An electrified fence and a watch kept through the hours of darkness were put in place, and the raids ceased at once.

units: there are two methods for watching wild birds
the first consists in setting out food to draw them in
this method quickly brings in the bolder species
it alters the behaviour of the very birds one claims to study
the second consists in sitting still inside a screen of cut branches
it calls for keeping quiet through a long wait
it shows behaviour that food never brings out
it is advised to begin with the first method and then take up the second
text: Before you carry your binoculars out to the hedge, settle on one of two ways of coming near the birds, because they do not show you the same thing. The first sets out food to draw them in: a handful of seed on a board, a lump of fat hung from a branch. Bold species will turn up quickly and counting them is easy, yet what you watch are guests at a table, not free birds. The second asks you to build a screen of cut branches, to sit inside it before first light, and to keep still and quiet. The wait drags on and on, and the cold works its way into you. In return you catch the display, the squabble over a dry stalk, the heavy flight of the bird bringing home nest stuff, things a feeding board never brings out. Start with the food until the shapes grow familiar; move to the hide once the names come to you without a pause.

units: a scientific team is finishing the yearly count of a colony of sea birds
the count is made on occupied nests and not on the adults in view
breeding numbers have fallen compared with the previous season
the fish these birds depend on has moved into deeper water
the adults range further to feed
the eggs are left alone more often than before
gulls take advantage of these absences to rob the nests
the team recommends limiting the access of walkers to the foot of the cliffs
text: A team of bird specialists is coming to the end of the yearly count of a colony lodged on the coastal cliffs, and their findings fall under four separate heads. Numbers first: the count is made on occupied nests, a steadier measure than the adults in view at any moment, and the total has fallen well below the figure of the previous season. Food next: the fish the birds live on has moved away into deeper water, which stretches out every feeding trip they make. Breeding after that: the adults range further out, eggs are left alone more often than before, and gulls with an eye for a chance come in and rob the uncovered nests. Access last: the team urges that the foot of the cliffs be closed to walkers through the delicate weeks, a step it calls modest in itself but open to immediate use.

units: the mare leaves her box as the gate opens
she halts and takes in the air before going forward
she shakes her whole coat to rid it of the damp
she rolls onto her back in a sandy hollow
she eats the grass of the field for a long stretch
she makes her way to the trough set under a tree
she stays on her feet and dozes in the shade of the leaves
she waits by the gate for someone to come and bring her in
text: As the gate swings open, the mare clears the doorway of her box and halts, nostrils wide, to take in the air of the field. She goes forward a few paces, then shakes herself out at length, and the damp of the night leaves her coat in a fine spray. Then comes the roll: she folds her forelegs, tips onto her flank, rubs her back into a sandy hollow, and rises again with a thrust of the loins. She grazes after that without lifting her head, moving on in short even steps along the fence, tearing at the lush growth of the edges and leaving the coarse tufts of the middle, until the heat turns her towards the trough set under the tree. There she drinks, and stays on her feet, one hind leg resting, eyelids heavy in the shade of the leaves. Late in the afternoon she comes back to the gate and waits, quite still, to be led in.

units: wildlife parks justify their existence by the rescue of species
their opponents hold that confinement undoes the animals
the surface available is far smaller than the ground covered in freedom
this restriction brings on repeated movements in meat-eaters
the food handed out removes all active searching
animals born in captivity survive poorly once released
the writer proposes keeping these parks for species that are truly at risk
the writer suggests funding the protection of wild places with the takings at the gate
text: Wildlife parks defend themselves by pointing to the rescue of species; their critics answer that shutting an animal in undoes the very creature it claims to save. The argument is worth following to its end, because one effect draws on the next. An enclosure, however roomy, gives a surface bearing no comparison with the ground a meat-eater covers when free. Out of that shrinking come the mechanical turns along the bars that keepers know so well. Food brought at fixed hours then removes all searching, and with it any schooling in the hunt. It follows that beasts born behind wire seldom last long once returned to the wild. The conclusion seems to me to hold: keep these parks for species that are truly at risk, and turn the takings at the gate over to the defence of wild places.
